content.title: About
content.content: A wheat bagel with raisins is a ring‑shaped baked good made from whole‑grain wheat flour, boiled briefly before baking to create a dense interior and a glossy crust. Raisins are folded into the dough, adding a subtle sweetness and fruity aroma. The result is a chewy, slightly sweet bagel with a crisp outer layer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine and were traditionally made with wheat flour.
Adding raisins is a modern twist that boosts nutrition and natural sweetness without extra sugar.
Boiling the dough before baking gives bagels their characteristic dense crumb and shiny crust.
Bagels are often served with cream cheese, smoked salmon, or simply butter.
In many countries the bagel is considered a classic breakfast or snack item.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat flour provides dietary fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals that support digestive health.

items.title: Natural sugars from raisins
items.content: Raisins supply quick‑acting energy and contain antioxidants such as polyphenols.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Both wheat and raisins contribute iron, essential for blood formation.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When baked properly, the bagel contains no trans fats, making it a heart‑friendlier choice.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may experience adverse reactions to the bagel.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins increase the natural sugar level, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bagels are carbohydrate‑rich and can be calorie‑dense, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Some recipes add salt to the dough; those watching sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bagel and spread cream cheese, nut butter, or avocado. It works well as a sandwich base with deli meat, vegetables, and greens. A warm bagel topped with a drizzle of honey and extra raisins makes a popular breakfast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bagel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Toast or warm in the oven before eating to restore the crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Toasted oat‑bran bread is a whole‑grain product made from wheat flour, oat bran, and a small amount of yeast. It has a crisp crust and a fragrant, slightly nutty flavor from the bran.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat bran is rich in beta‑glucan, which helps lower cholesterol levels.
Toasting enhances aroma and creates a crunchier crust.
Oat bran is often added to bread to boost nutritional value without dramatically changing taste.
This type of bread is popular in diet plans because of its high fiber content.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oat bran increases both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Beta‑glucan from oat bran can reduce LDL (“bad”) cholesterol.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: The bread provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains magnesium, iron, and zinc, which aid muscle function and immune health.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The combination of whole grains and bran slows carbohydrate absorption, helpful for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Despite its benefits, the bread is calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Bran contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread as a snack, for sandwiches, toasted with toppings, alongside soups, or use it to make breadcrumbs for casseroles. Toasting brings out extra flavor and crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or cloth sack. For longer storage keep it in an airtight container in the refrigerator, though the crust may lose some crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Brussels sprouts are small cabbage-like buds belonging to the Brassicaceae family. Native to the Mediterranean region, they are now cultivated in many temperate areas worldwide. When cooked (boiled, steamed, or roasted) they retain a mild bitterness, a sweet aroma, and a crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vegetable gets its name from Brussels, Belgium, where it was cultivated on a large scale in the 16th century.
In the 18th century it was called “little cabbage,” and in Russia it is often referred to as “cabbage‑minute.”
Raw sprouts contain glucoraphanin, which can cause gas, but heat treatment breaks it down.
They are rich in antioxidants, including vitamin C and carotenoids.
There are over 300 varieties of Brussels sprouts, differing in size and leaf color.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One serving provides more than 100 % of the daily value for vitamin C, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Provides folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Brussels sprouts contain quercetin and kaempferol, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Raw sprouts can cause abdominal gas due to oligosaccharides; cooking reduces this effect.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High vitamin K content may diminish the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergy to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brussels sprouts can be boiled, steamed, sautéed with olive oil and garlic, or roasted until caramelized. Before cooking, trim the tough stem and discard outer leaves. They pair well with nuts, dried fruit, or a drizzle of balsamic vinegar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sprouts in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container, where they stay fresh for up to 10 days. Do not wash before storing to avoid excess moisture. For long‑term storage, freeze cooked sprouts in an airtight bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Ramen bowl with beef is a ready‑to‑cook package that includes ramen noodles, a flavored broth packet and dried beef pieces. The kit also contains dried vegetables and seasoning. Add boiling water, stir and wait 3‑5 minutes for a hot, satisfying meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ramen originated in Japan in the early 20th century, but its roots trace back to Chinese wheat noodles.
Beef in ramen is often marinated in soy sauce, mirin and spices, giving the dish a rich umami flavor.
Dry ramen kits are popular for travel and office lunches because they require no refrigeration.
Japan boasts over 10,000 regional ramen varieties, each with its own broth style.
Ramen broth can be based on pork, chicken, soy sauce, miso or salt.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Beef and noodles provide complete protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Electrolytes
items.content: The broth packet often adds sodium and potassium, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and seasonings deliver B12, B6 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: A single package offers a defined calorie count, useful for those monitoring intake.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Broth packets can be very salty, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product may contain soy, gluten in the noodles, and food additives that can trigger allergies.

items.title: Quality of beef
items.content: Dried beef pieces may include preservatives; choose brands with minimal additives.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Some ramen varieties use fatty broths, increasing the dish’s calorie density.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour hot (not boiling) water over the contents, stir, and let sit for 3‑5 minutes. Optionally top with fresh vegetables, herbs, a boiled egg or extra soy sauce for added flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dry components in a cool, dry place, sealed tightly after opening. Use an airtight container. Do not leave the prepared broth at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

roll-whole-grain-white-hot-dog-bun.title: Whole Grain White Hot Dog Bun

content.title: About
content.content: The whole grain white hot dog bun (item 2515) is a soft, slightly sweet roll made from a blend of wheat and whole‑grain flours. Perfect for hot dogs, sandwiches and quick snacks. It provides about 45 g of carbohydrates and 5 g of protein per 100 g.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The whole‑grain version retains more dietary fiber than a standard white bun.
Its white color comes from a modest amount of sugar and milk, which tenderizes the dough.
These buns are popular in fast‑food because they steam quickly in a steamer or microwave.
Sometimes seeds such as sunflower or pumpkin are added for extra flavor and crunch.

items.title: Higher dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour supplies more fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: The combination of whole grains and limited sugar gives a milder blood‑sugar response than regular white buns.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron and magnesium that help muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made with wheat, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is added for flavor; those monitoring sodium intake should consider this.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The bun contains about 250 kcal per 100 g, so portion control is advisable for calorie‑restricted diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bun lengthwise, place a hot dog, and add mustard, ketchup, pickles, onions or lettuce. Toasting on a grill or in a toaster gives a crisp crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a cool, dry place in the original packaging. Once opened, transfer to an airtight bag and use within 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze up to 2 months.
